newsitem.title: UK: ERM bands - Why 15 percent isn't 15 percent.
newsitem.headline: ERM bands - Why 15 percent isn't 15 percent.

text.p: The fluctuation limits within the European exchange rate mechanism (ERM) -- both the so called 15 percent bands, or the narrower 2.25 percent limits -- do not work out exactly either side of the central rate.
This is basically because the inverse of the upper limit of, say, mark/lira must equal the lower limit in lira/mark.
Simply, a 10 percent rise of the mark against the lira does not equal a 10 percent fall in the lira against the mark.

For example, if you take mark/lira at 1,000 lira per mark and there is a 10 percent rally you end up with 1,100. The mark is 100 lira higher. But if you invert this in terms of the lira/mark rate you start with 0.001 marks per lira, and a 10 percent move down would be equal to a move to 0.0009 marks per lira.
Invert this, by dividing it into one, and you get 1,111.11 and it is this anomaly which must be allowed for when making sure the upper end of mark/lira equals its inverse in lira/mark.
For the mathematicians among you the EU Commission's guide follows -
Let x be the central ERM rate of for example mark per French franc.
Then 1/x is the central rate of French franc per mark.
The total band width is 30% or 0.3.
The following conditions must be satisfied:
x(1+ru) to the power of -1 = (1/x)(1-rl)
ie. the inverse of the upper limit in mark per French franc must equal the lower limit in French franc per mark.
and....ru + rl = 0.3 ie. the total band-width equals 30%
where..ru is the upper range and rl is the lower range.
Putting the two conditions together yields the following quadratic equation:
ru squared + 1.7ru - 0.3 =0
The solution to this is:
ru = 0.161187 (or +16.1187% as the upper range)
rl = 0.138813 (or -13.8813% as the lower range)
